title: Cloudflare’s Auto Router Rates Each Request for Stakes, from the Most Recent Turns
gist: Cloudflare launched Auto Router in public beta on AI Gateway, a classifier that picks a model per request using task, complexity, ambiguity, stakes and context dependence; InfoQ highlights a benchmark where it loses to a top model, the author calls the trade ten points of reliability for roughly a third of the spend, and practitioners raise risk-labelling and stale-weights concerns.

insights.claim: Auto Router first builds a candidate pool by filtering models on request format, credentials, billing, access control and spend limits, then a multi-head classifier on Workers AI assigns probabilities over 14 task categories and rates complexity, ambiguity, stakes and context dependence 1 to 5.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Model routing is becoming a managed infrastructure layer, positioning gateways as control points in AI spend.

insights.claim: Models are scored under the stated formula utility = expected quality - adaptive cost penalty, with price weighted less as difficulty rises, and classification uses only the newest turns, capped at 8 KiB of text.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Cost-versus-quality tradeoffs are encoded as policy, with recent-turn truncation as a design compromise.
insights.quote: utility = expected quality - adaptive cost penalty.

insights.claim: The response carries cf-aig-routed-model and cf-aig-routing-reason headers with values like cost_optimal_within_pool and pinned_by_turn, so routing is auditable, and pools can be restricted per request via allowed-models and allowed-providers headers but not as saved routing profiles.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Auditability helps compliance use cases, but missing saved profiles is a gap for enterprise governance.

insights.claim: A cheaper model is not a saving if someone has to spend another hour fixing the result, so the relevant measure is quality-adjusted cost.
insights.speaker: Jacques B
insights.so_what: Model routing should be judged on cost per accepted outcome, not on token price.
insights.quote: A cheaper model isn’t much of a saving if someone has to spend another hour fixing the result.
insights.locator: Jacques B, a CTO working on agentic engineering

insights.claim: Cloudflare published a benchmark across 97 tasks with three samples per model and 10,000 bootstrap resamples where its own router loses to a top model, which the author summarizes as ten points of reliability for roughly a third of the spend and a choice teams can make.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Vendor candour about the quality gap makes the cost-saving claim more credible, but the table itself is not reproduced in the article.
insights.quote: Ten points of reliability for roughly a third of the spend.

insights.claim: On Reddit, reachjalil argued auto routers end up costing more for less intelligence and that a capable model is cheaper if outcomes matter, while yangqi countered that the unit should be the task, not the request.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The debate over routing versus single strong models turns on how cost is measured.

insights.claim: Because stakes are scored from recent turns, a long agent session where the user says early that it is a customer refund and later just says go ahead may be downgraded, so Igor Pyrin would carry an application-owned risk label across turns to decide whether cloudflare/auto can be used at all.
insights.speaker: Igor Pyrin
insights.so_what: Agent safety needs risk state outside the router, since the committing turn is often the least informative.
insights.quote: A short final instruction should not silently lower the risk classification of the underlying action.
insights.locator: In a long agent session, the user may say

insights.claim: Without a session ID, requests in the same conversation may hit different models and cannot reuse the prompt cache, so Cloudflare applies a switching penalty that grows with context length since a new model may redo reasoning tokens at output prices.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Hidden cache and reasoning costs can erode routing savings in long sessions.
insights.locator: Session handling carries a cost too

insights.claim: Routing weights come from benchmark results, so new models must be added to the scoring matrix by hand, and weights go stale with constantly changing models.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Maintenance lag on rapidly shifting model leaderboards is a structural weakness of benchmark-based routers.
insights.quote: especially with the constantly changing models

insights.claim: The default pool lists Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Fable 5 alongside GPT-5.6 Luna, Sol and Terra and Grok 4.5, while the two baselines in the benchmark table, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol, sit in the opt-in list, so teams reproducing the benchmark should confirm what their gateway actually selects.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The benchmark's headline comparison may not describe default production behavior.
insights.locator: Worth checking before trusting the figures

insights.claim: Auto Router is free during the beta with no stated pricing afterward, does not support WebSockets (only Chat Completions and Responses API), and a cloudflare/auto-best option with the same classifier will choose highest expected quality without cost tradeoff.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Post-beta pricing is a key unknown for whether gateway-level routing becomes a revenue line.
insights.locator: Auto Router is free during the beta
